# Answer

**They passed BEHIND the boat on the left** — i.e. on its far side, further from the
camera — not between that boat and the camera.

## What is in the picture

The photograph shows a flooded city street (the corner building is lettered
"MORT HARPER AND COMPANY / ORIENTAL MILLS"). The subject of the question is the
lone figure in a white shirt and dark hat, sitting low in a small boat in the
middle of the flooded roadway, roughly in the centre of the frame. "The boat on
the left" is the small craft over near the left-hand row of buildings, well up
the street, which has one person standing in it and another seated.

## Step 1 — Which way was the rower travelling?

The seated figure is facing the camera. I checked this at the pixel level: the
hat brim, head and shoulders are symmetric about the same vertical axis, and the
shoulders are at their full apparent width (about 19–20 px, which at the local
image scale is roughly 0.5 m). A body turned away from square-on would show
narrower shoulders and an off-centre head. So the person is square-on to the lens.

A person *rowing* sits facing the stern, and the boat travels bow-first — that
is, the direction of travel is behind the rower's back. Because this rower's back
is turned away from the camera, the boat was moving **away from the camera**,
further up the flooded street.

## Step 2 — What was the heading of that straight-line course?

The boat itself is seen end-on, not broadside. The dark hull under the rower
measures about 26 px across and about 16 px from gunwale to waterline — almost
as tall as it is wide. A rowing boat seen side-on at that distance would be
several times longer than that; even a 10° angle off dead-on would make it
noticeably wider than what is visible. So the hull's long axis lies essentially
along the camera's line of sight to it.

Combining Steps 1 and 2: the rower was pulling almost straight away from the
camera position, receding up the street on a line that barely changes bearing.

## Step 3 — Where does that line go relative to the boat on the left?

Two things place the boat on the left elsewhere:

- **It is much further away.** Its waterline sits far higher in the frame
  (around y ≈ 470) than the rower's (around y ≈ 528), and the people in it are
  roughly a third the apparent size of the rower. On the flat water plane that
  makes it something like two to three times the rower's distance from the camera.
- **It is well off to the left.** It sits around x ≈ 330 in the frame, while the
  rower sits around x ≈ 633, a separation of roughly 14° of bearing.

A course running almost radially away from the camera keeps the rower on his own
bearing, to the right of the left-hand boat, while his distance from the camera
grows without limit. He therefore reaches and then exceeds the left-hand boat's
distance while still off to its right, and the point where his track finally
crosses the camera's sight-line to that boat lies far beyond it. For his course
to have passed *in front of* the left-hand boat instead, it would have had to be
angled more than about 20–25° to the left of the camera axis — and at that angle
his hull would appear markedly oblique and several times wider than it actually
does in the photograph.

## Step 4 — The conclusion does not depend on which way along the line he went

This is worth stating explicitly, because the front/behind question is really a
question about the *line* of travel, not the direction along it. Even if one
rejected the "rowers face backwards" reasoning and assumed instead that he was
coming towards the camera, he would have been travelling along that same
near-radial line — meaning he would have come from much further up the street
than the left-hand boat, and so would still have been on that boat's far side
when he went past it.

## Answer

**Behind.** Rowing in a constant direction, the seated rower's track passed on the
far side of the boat on the left — further from the camera than that boat — so he
went behind it rather than in front of it.

Caveat: the print is soft and the figure is small, so the heading is established
from the end-on shape of the hull and the square-on pose of the rower rather than
from a crisply visible bow or wake (the water is glassy and no wake is legible).
The margin is large, though: the boat would have to be turned far more steeply to
the left than it appears for the answer to flip to "in front of".

# Answer

**They passed IN FRONT of the boat on the left** (on the camera's side of it, between the camera and that boat), not behind it.

# Which boats are meant

- **The rowboat / the seated person:** the lone figure in the middle of the flooded street, directly in front of the "Oriental Mills" building. It is a person in a dark hat and white shirt, seated in a very low, dark boat that is seen end-on, so the hull is barely visible above the water. The figure is squarely facing the camera.
- **The boat on the left:** the white rowing boat in the left background, level with the far shopfronts, carrying a standing man (working an oar or pole) and two seated passengers. It is far up the street, much farther from the camera than the centre rowboat (it sits higher in the frame, at the far waterline, and its occupants are smaller).

# Reasoning, point by point

1. **A rower faces backwards.** Someone rowing a boat sits facing the stern and pulls the oars, so the boat travels bow-first, away from the direction the rower is looking. The rower always faces where they have come from.

2. **This rower faces the camera.** Zooming in shows the face shadowed under the hat brim, the white shirt front, and the arms held forward in the lap. Therefore the boat is travelling away from the camera, toward the Oriental Mills building, and it came from the camera's side of the scene, i.e. from the foreground.

3. **The water confirms this.** After removing the vertical building reflections from the water (high-pass / detrended contrast enhancement), the only disturbed, rippled water in the whole picture is a broad trail running from the centre rowboat down toward the lower-left foreground of the photo. Fine streaks in that trail run diagonally up-right and converge on the rowboat's position. That is the boat's wake, so the boat came from the lower-left foreground and is heading up and to the right, away from the camera, exactly as the rower's posture implies. Everywhere else the flood water is glassy and undisturbed.

4. **Extrapolate the constant heading backwards.** Rowing in a constant direction means a straight track. Running that track backwards from the rowboat leads down and to the left, toward the camera. When the rowboat was level with the white boat's position on the left, it was in the near foreground, far closer to the camera than the white boat, which is up at the far end of the street. The rowboat's track therefore lay between the camera and the boat on the left.

5. **Conclusion.** The seated rower crossed the foreground in front of the boat on the left. They did not pass behind it. (A viewer who assumed the rower was travelling toward the camera would wrongly conclude the boat had come from the background, i.e. from behind the left-hand boat; the rowing posture rules that out.)

# Note on the other boats in the picture

Beside the white boat, in the left background, there is a second small rowing boat with a single seated rower and a third, darker boat with three seated people in front of the Oriental Mills corner. The conclusion above holds for any of these as "the boat on the left", because all of them are far up the street and the centre rowboat's track came from the near foreground.

If, however, the question intends "the rowboat" to be that second small background boat (the one with the lone rower and visible oars, immediately to the right of the white boat) and "the boat on the left" to be the white boat next to it, the answer would be different: that small boat's bow points right and its rower faces left toward the stern, so it is moving right and has already gone past the white boat; its waterline sits slightly higher in the frame than the white boat's and its rower appears smaller, so it is a little farther from the camera and its straight track passed behind the white boat. My primary reading, though, is the prominent seated figure in the centre rowboat, for which the answer is in front.
